I am not sure what an attacker could do with that info tho, organise a hard fork to keep the pow chain going? (if it can only be measured once a week) Can't use the the ETH1 blockhash because miners can manipulate it. 🤔 well I suppose you could still use the blockhash.. but just not that of the previous block.. but a block that was 100 blocks ago... The random merge is only a source of stress for the developers, not the community, we could have some sort of system that let's the devs trigger the merge without warning

Have a smart contract on the pow chain that triggers the merge, it can be triggered by a multisig controlled by the devs, eth1 fork choice changes so it switches to pos once it sees the state on the contract change

The contract could take a parameter that requires a given blockhash for one of the previous blocks, this would avoid the scenario where an attacker takes the transaction and replays it on an arbitrary large forked chain

excerpts.author: underbasic
excerpts.content: the way I am looking at it, the security problem is about the sheer size of the pool of hardware that secures/can attack the network, so 1. Removing ASICS, 2. Increasing DAG over time should slowly reduce that number to something more managable

excerpts.author: underbasic
excerpts.content: Does that make any sense?

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: A proposal to prioritize the merge after London is submitted https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/278

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: Reducing the amount of hashpower that is able to keep mining Ethereum does make sense. Doesn't increasing the DAG and pushing ASICS out of the game make centralisation vector more severe?

excerpts.author: underbasic
excerpts.content: how does it do that, unless we presume that the bigger more expensive GPUs are all held centrally?

excerpts.author: underbasic
excerpts.content: (by bigger and more expensive I mean by memory size)

excerpts.author: underbasic
excerpts.content: if you have something like the difficulty bomb but for the dag, it increases by 1gb every x blocks or something, then eventually forks HAVE to happen or everyone gets kicked off, it seems a better idea than the difficulty bomb that grinds the network to a halt

excerpts.author: butta
excerpts.content: what are the trade offs between a _slow_ and _quick_ merge? has this been discussed somewhere?

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: primarily complexity which reduces both time and risk. "quick merge" just means minimal complexity at point of merge with iterative feature upgrades from there

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: risk as in if you try to do too much at once, there is additional consensus risk

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: e.g. adding validator withdrawals at time of merge is essentially a large EVM feature in addition to the consensus feature

excerpts.author: butta
excerpts.content: right, reading benjaminion’s recent post he said that a quick merge would cause a delay with the further steps/phases if i am not mistaken ?

excerpts.author: butta
excerpts.content:
<https://hackmd.io/@benjaminion/eth2_news/https%3A%2F%2Fhackmd.io%2F%40benjaminion%2Fwnie2_210313> 
> If we are genuinely ok with this—with data sharding, with most of the roadmap potentially being delayed for years, with technical debt that could linger forever—then, yes, let’s rush to get Eth1 onto Proof of Stake.

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: We have to do one or the other first. Doing sharding first has extremely minimal (if any) value to the ethereum ecosystem if done before the merge

excerpts.author: butta
excerpts.content:
From a PR standpoint i believe rushing PoS without scaling will be bad, because a scalable chain was promoted along with PoS for the past years. 
Not a technical argument but worth considering

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content: As a counter-point, I think that PoS first will have better optics due to reducing energy usage.  This is certainly becoming a major factor with the people I speak to regarding blockchains.
